claims.text: The unmodified elemental-Cr-coated zirconium-alloy cladding is prone to premature failure caused by Cr–Zr interdiffusion at elevated temperatures.
The proposed intervention is an approximately 50 nm ZrN interlayer deposited by reactive sputtering between the zirconium alloy and the elemental Cr coating.
A roughly 50 nm ZrN interlayer will significantly reduce elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Reducing Cr–Zr interdiffusion with the ZrN interlayer will prevent premature coating failure.
The ZrN-modified coating will retain protective performance in subcritical water below 400°C for durations of up to thousands of hours.
The ZrN-modified coating will retain protective performance in steam at approximately 1200°C for up to one hour.
ZrN will act as a stable and chemically inert interfacial barrier under the specified environments.
The ZrN interlayer will maintain a sharp interface by restricting atomic transport between the zirconium-alloy substrate and Cr coating.
The ZrN interlayer will inhibit grain-boundary diffusion between the zirconium-alloy substrate and Cr coating.
At elevated temperatures, ZrN will suppress the effective diffusion coefficients of Cr and Zr.
Suppression of Cr and Zr diffusion will occur because ZrN limits grain-boundary- and defect-mediated diffusion pathways.
Reduced Cr and Zr mobility will prevent or significantly delay formation of deleterious intermetallic compounds.
Preventing or delaying intermetallic formation will preserve the integrity of the protective Cr layer.
Relative to Cr deposited directly on zirconium alloy, the ZrN-modified system will show markedly less Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, the ZrN-modified system will retain a more intact and well-defined interface.
Protective performance under accident conditions is contingent on the ZrN barrier remaining intact and stable.
The long-term stability of a nanoscale ZrN layer in high-temperature steam is uncertain.
